signals.title: Optimized support for Open NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL | Red Hat Developer
signals.excerpt:
Red Hat AI is releasing optimized FP8 and DSpark speculative decoding checkpoints for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal mixture-of-experts (MoE) model built for long-running agents. These checkpoints are designed to double inference throughput on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs without compromising output accuracy.

These optimizations combine FP8 quantization using LLM Compressor with a DSpark speculative decoding model trained using Speculators, delivering substantial inference performance gains while preserving model quality.
...
To accelerate inference for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, we are releasing an optimized FP8-quantized checkpoint. FP8 quantization reduces the precision of model weights and activations from BF16 to 8-bit floating point, cutting model weight memory and storage requirements in half while preserving model quality.

FP8 quantization is particularly effective on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, which feature native FP8 Tensor Core support and deliver approximately 2× higher theoretical matrix multiplication throughput compared to BF16. Combined with reduced memory bandwidth requirements, this enables higher inference throughput and improved GPU efficiency, especially for large-scale models.

We generated the quantized checkpoints using the LLM Compressor library and its model-free post-training quantization (PTQ) workflow, leveraging the calibration-free nature of FP8 Dynamic quantization.

After evaluating several quantization configurations, we settled on quantizing the attention, expert, and Mamba projection layers of the main model, while keeping the shared experts, routers, normalization layers, and `lm_head` in their original precision. For the multi-token prediction (MTP) layers, we quantized the attention, expert, and shared expert layers, while leaving the normalization layers and `eh_proj` unquantized.
...
To assess the impact of quantization on model accuracy, particularly in reasoning-intensive tasks and agentic workflows, we evaluate both the BF16 and FP8 models across a broad suite of representative benchmarks. To ensure a fair and consistent comparison, both models are evaluated under identical conditions: non-greedy sampling, four NVIDIA H200 GPUs, vLLM 0.31.0, and the Inspect AI and Harbor evaluation frameworks. The evaluation results are presented in Figure 1. The FP8 checkpoint consistently preserves model accuracy across all evaluated benchmarks.
...
The performance gains from quantized checkpoints can be further extended by enabling speculative decoding with parallel drafting DSpark models. Speculative decoding accelerates inference by using a smaller, faster draft model to propose multiple tokens ahead of time, which the LLM then verifies in parallel.
...
Quantization and speculative decoding are complementary, orthogonal inference acceleration techniques that can be combined to achieve compounded performance gains. To demonstrate their individual and combined impact, we conducted a series of benchmarks using vLLM, highlighting the performance improvements enabled by each optimization and the additional benefits of combining them.

The following plots (Figure 3, Figure 4, and Figure 5) demonstrate performance benchmarking, comparing the performance gains achieved through swapping MTP speculative decoding with our trained DSpark speculator as well as swapping the BF16 checkpoint for our FP8 quantized checkpoint. All benchmarks were performed on four H100s across workloads with prompts from various datasets. Each chart shows per-user streaming speed (interactivity) on the x-axis versus total output throughput (tok/s) on the y-axis, with each point representing a different concurrency level N. The HumanEval prompts come from OpenAI's HumanEval coding benchmark, while the math_reasoning and RAG prompts come from Spec-Bench, the ACL 2024 speculative decoding benchmark suite.

Each upgrade delivers meaningful gains on its own, and they compose cleanly. Swapping MTP for our trained DSpark speculator at BF16 primarily boosts single-user streaming speed, while swapping the BF16 checkpoint for FP8 primarily boosts aggregate throughput under load, where its reduced compute and memory footprint matters most. Combining them outperforms either intermediate configuration at every concurrency level on both workloads.
...

...
Reflection designed Beam (~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M-token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks.

Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step.
...
First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck. Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users.

Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity. Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls.

To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang).
...
To run Beam’s BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle.
...
- Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control.
- Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance): Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation.
- Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory (Tier 1), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs (Tier 2) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch.
...
A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure.
...
Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously:

- Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales.
- KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput.
- Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity.
- Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast.
...

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. Google has introduced support for local models in the Antigravity SDK, enabling developers to build and execute agentic workflows directly on their own machines, while retaining the flexibility to mix in cloud-based models for higher-level tasks. This approach gives developers greater control over data privacy, inference costs, network dependencies, and computational workload distribution.

One of the most compelling capabilities of the Antigravity SDK is hybrid agent orchestration, which adapts Google's proposed Architect-Builder pattern to a mixed cloud-local compute environment.
...
Google says that the Antigravity SDK enables the architect to operate in the cloud, devising a strategy and breaking the task into smaller units using filenames and task descriptions, without requiring access to the source code itself. The builders, instead, run locally and perform tasks such as reproducing security vulnerabilities, proposing code fixes, reviewing candidate patches, and running regression tests. Additional specialized local agents can validate proposed changes against the provided test suites, keeping the code-intensive stages of the workflow on-device.
...
The initial implementation focuses on running Gemma 4 26B A4B through Google's LiteRT technology. However, developers are not limited to LiteRT exclusively, as the Antigravity SDK also supports OpenAI-compatible local inference servers through `LocalOpenAIAgentConfig`, including Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.
...
The Antigravity SDK should not be confused with the Antigravity IDE, which is an IDE powered by the Antigravity SDK.
